newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drill sergeant pleads guilty, awaits sentence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drill sergeant pleads guilty, awaits sentence.

text.p: A drill sergeant faced dishonourable discharge and possible imprisonment on Wednesday after admitting to having sex with three female recruits in the latest sexual misconduct scandal to rock the military.

At a court martial on Tuesday at the Fort Leonard Wood Army base in Missouri, Staff Sgt. Loren Taylor pleaded guilty to seven charges of misconduct. In exchange, prosecutors agreed to drop charges of obstruction of justice and perjury.
Taylor also said he tried to have sex with another recruit and admitted that he had improper contact with a fifth recruit, whom he told: "No one will find out."

The guilty plea came a day after the Army disclosed that Taylor and two other noncommissioned officers at Fort Leonard Wood were facing charges ranging from consensual intercourse to indecent assault. Seven other drill sergeants at the base were suspended pending investigations.
The Army said the latest charges resulted from ongoing investigations and were not related to the unfolding rape and sexual harassment scandal at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.
Army regulations forbid all sexual relationships between commanders and subordinates.

Taylor, who was due to be sentenced on Wednesday, faced a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison, dishonourable discharge and loss of pay. But Brad Rose, a base spokesman, said it was "not likely" Taylor's penalty would be that severe.
About 25,000 troops train at Fort Leonard Wood each year, making it the second-largest of four posts where the Army conducts basic training.
Col. Carl Strock, chief of staff at the base, told a news conference Tuesday the cases were "disturbing" but the Army still had confidence in its procedures and chain of command.
"We acknowledge that we must do better," Strock said. "Sexual harassment is an area of zero tolerance but unfortunately, as in any human enterprise, we are not a zero-defect institution."

Unlike the Maryland investigation, none of the Missouri cases involved charges of rape or forcible sodomy. The alleged offences occurred between the summers of 1995 and 1996 and appeared to be unrelated, the Army said.

Last week three male Army trainers were charged in a rape and sexual harassment case involving alleged attacks on women recruits in Maryland. About 20 people were suspended from their duties at the Maryland base pending an investigation.

Pentagon officials feared the scandal would give the U.S. military another black eye after a string of harassment cases that began with the 1991 "Tailhook" scandal, in which male Navy and Marine pilots fondled women at a Las Vegas hotel.
